passage: On the farm track Tushar, two, sat on his mother's hip and stabbed a finger at a black shape by the pond. "Bhains!" Ganga stopped. "Yes, bhains. A big black bhains." He pointed again, this time at a crow. "Kau!" "Crow, yes," she said, laughing. He kept on, one point at a time, looking back at her each time to see her face.

qa.q: What animals did Tushar point at?
qa.a: He pointed at a buffalo (bhains) and then at a crow.

qa.q: Why does Tushar keep looking back at Ganga, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: He is probably excited about what he spots and wants to check that Ganga is sharing it too. He might also be checking whether she will keep giving him attention.

qa.q: What could Ganga add to help his language grow?
qa.a: She can name each thing back, add one small detail such as colour or sound, and pause for him. 😊

qa.q: How might Ganga feel as Tushar points at one thing after another?
qa.a: Ganga seems amused and happy to join in, since she laughs and names each thing back to him.

grounding: A toddler points and names objects to share attention, and an adult names them back.

passage: In the playground in Toronto, Soo-ah, two, pointed to a red bus and called out "Bus!" Her mother Leila crouched. "Yes, a bus, a red bus." Soo-ah then pointed to a shape in the grass and said something like "dah." Leila followed her finger. "A dog? Is that a dog?" Soo-ah nodded hard and clapped, watching Leila's face.

qa.q: What did Soo-ah say when she pointed at the red vehicle?
qa.a: She said "Bus!"

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's clapping suggest about her feelings, and what else might explain it?
qa.a: It suggests she is pleased to be understood and to share what she saw. She might also just enjoy the dog itself.

qa.q: How could Leila keep helping Soo-ah's vocabulary?
qa.a: She can keep naming back what Soo-ah points to, guess kindly at unclear words, and add a small detail.

qa.q: How might Leila see Soo-ah's pointing?
qa.a: She likely sees it as an invitation to look together, not just a request for a word.

grounding: A toddler points and names objects to share attention, and an adult who names back builds vocabulary.

passage: I'm Thomas. I live on the floor above Nikita's family. On Saturday, on the stairs, Nikita stopped and pointed down at the landing. "Ca! Ca!" A white cat was curled there. Her mother said, "Cat! A white cat." Nikita said, "Ca," again, very pleased, then pointed at my shoes. "Shoo!" Her mother laughed. "Yes, shoes!" I don't know how many words she knows. She seemed to want us all to look.

qa.q: What was curled on the landing?
qa.a: A white cat.

qa.q: What might Nikita be feeling as she pointed and named things?
qa.a: She seemed pleased and excited to share what she noticed, wanting everyone to look.

qa.q: What did Nikita's mother do that helps Nikita's vocabulary?
qa.a: She named back what Nikita pointed at, "Cat! A white cat" and "shoes", adding words.

qa.q: How does Thomas experience the moment?
qa.a: Thomas seems amused and charmed at being included when she points at the shoes.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler point and name things to share interest, and her mother names them back.

passage:
Sunday night: Amandeep pointed out of the window. "Oon!" Urmila, his grandmother, said, "Moon! Big round moon."
Wednesday: on the road, he pointed and shouted, "Ta!" as a tractor went by. "Tractor!" said Urmila. "Red tractor."
The next Sunday: Amandeep took Urmila's hand, pulled her to the window, pointed up and said, "Moon!"

qa.q: What went by on the road on Wednesday?
qa.a: A red tractor.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when he pulled Urmila to the window?
qa.a: He was excited and proud to share the moon with her, wanting her to look with him.

qa.q: What habit of Urmila's helped Amandeep?
qa.a: She named back each thing he pointed at, adding a detail like "big round" or "red".

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Amandeep says "Moon!" himself?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and delighted, seeing the word he learned from her. 🙂

grounding: Over a week a toddler points and names things, and his grandmother names back until he uses the full word.

passage:
At the fruit market in Mumbai, Chandrika was bargaining over mangoes. Sonali, on her hip, pointed at a pile of bananas. "Nana! Nana!"
Chandrika kept talking. Sonali tugged her collar. "Nana!"
Chandrika stopped, turned and looked. "Banana! Yellow bananas." Sonali beamed and pointed at the next pile. "Mmm?" "Mangoes," said Chandrika, and the fruit seller laughed.

qa.q: What was Chandrika bargaining over?
qa.a: Mangoes.

qa.q: Why did Sonali tug Chandrika's collar?
qa.a: She wanted her mother to notice and share what she'd found, feeling ignored while Chandrika bargained.

qa.q: What changed when Chandrika stopped to name the bananas?
qa.a: Sonali felt heard and kept sharing, and got new words for each fruit.

qa.q: How might the fruit seller see the moment?
qa.a: The seller seems amused, enjoying Sonali naming the fruit.

grounding: A mother stops to name back what her toddler points at, and the child keeps sharing.

passage:
“Bus!” Trisha pointed from the pram.
“Yes, a big red bus!” said Dolma.
“Dog!”
“A sleepy dog, under the cart.”
“Moon!”
Dolma looked up. “You're right, there's the moon, in the daytime!”
“She's been chattering nonstop,” said Grandpa, walking beside them.
“I love it,” said Dolma. “She's telling us what she sees.”
Trisha pointed again. “Ba-loon!”
“Blue balloon,” said Dolma, grinning.

qa.q: Where was the dog?
qa.a: The sleepy dog was under the cart.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling as she kept pointing and naming things?
qa.a: She was excited and eager to share what caught her interest, and Dolma's answers kept her going.

qa.q: What does Dolma do that helps Trisha's vocabulary?
qa.a: She names each thing back with a little more detail, like "a big red bus" and "blue balloon."

qa.q: How does Grandpa see Trisha's pointing and naming?
qa.a: Grandpa sees it as nonstop chattering, a bit much, while Dolma enjoys it.

grounding: It shows a toddler pointing and naming objects to share attention, and an adult naming back to build her vocabulary.
